intro: From the Anthropic 'Building Effective Agents' guide. Each pattern is a separate solution shape — pick the simplest one that does the job. Do not reach for the plain agent loop when a 30-line prompt chain would do.

items.title: Prompt chaining
items.whenToUse: The task decomposes into a fixed, ordered sequence of sub-steps. No branching.
items.mechanism: Output of LLM call N becomes input to LLM call N+1. Optional gates between steps (regex match, validator) catch derailment early.
items.tradeoff: Cheap, deterministic, easy to debug. Brittle if task shape varies. Always your first try.

items.title: Routing
items.whenToUse: Distinct sub-categories of input each need different downstream handling (different prompts, models, or tools).
items.mechanism: Classifier LLM (small/cheap) emits one of N labels. Each label maps to a specialized handler.
items.tradeoff: Concentrates the hard model spend where it matters. Adds one extra hop of latency. The /ask page itself is a routing pattern.

items.title: Parallelization (sectioning + voting)
items.whenToUse: Sectioning: independent sub-problems run in parallel. Voting: same problem N times with different prompts; majority wins.
items.mechanism: Fan-out → parallel LLM calls → aggregate. Sectioning aggregates by concat; voting aggregates by tally or judge.
items.tradeoff: Wall-clock latency drops. Cost multiplies. Voting buys robustness on borderline classifications at N× cost.

items.title: Orchestrator-workers
items.whenToUse: Task structure is dynamic and only known at run time (e.g. 'change every file that references X').
items.mechanism: Orchestrator LLM plans sub-tasks at run time and dispatches each to a worker. Workers report back; orchestrator synthesizes.
items.tradeoff: Flexible but slow and expensive. Easy to misuse — try chaining or routing first.

items.title: Evaluator-optimizer
items.whenToUse: Iterative refinement against measurable quality (translation polish, code that must compile).
items.mechanism: Generator LLM produces output → evaluator LLM (or program) critiques → generator revises. Loop until evaluator approves or max-iter.
items.tradeoff: Quality climbs visibly. Cost is N× a single call. Evaluator must be sharper than generator on the dimension being graded — otherwise it just rubber-stamps.

items.title: Plain agent loop
items.whenToUse: Open-ended task with unpredictable steps and tool use (research, coding, browsing).
items.mechanism: Think → tool → observe → repeat. Covered in depth in Module F.
items.tradeoff: Maximum flexibility, maximum cost, maximum failure surface. The pattern of last resort, not first.

items.title: Extended thinking with tools
items.whenToUse: Tasks where reasoning between tool calls is load-bearing (math, multi-hop research, planning).
items.mechanism: Enable extended-thinking on Sonnet/Opus. Model emits thinking blocks between each tool call, visible in the trace.
items.tradeoff: Fewer, deeper steps. Higher per-step cost. Reduces total step count enough to often pay for itself.

pitfalls.title: Reaching for the agent loop first
pitfalls.body: A 200-line agent loop replaced what a 20-line prompt chain would have done. Always try the simpler pattern first — agent loops are expensive and hard to debug.

pitfalls.title: Voting without diversity
pitfalls.body: Running the same prompt 5× at the same temperature gets 5 nearly-identical answers. For voting to work, vary prompts, models, or temperatures meaningfully.

pitfalls.title: Evaluator that rubber-stamps
pitfalls.body: If the evaluator is the same model + same prompt as the generator, it will approve almost everything. Use a different model, a checklist, or a programmatic check.

pitfalls.title: Orchestrator runaway
pitfalls.body: Orchestrator keeps decomposing sub-tasks into sub-sub-tasks. Cap recursion depth + budget per dispatch.

pitfalls.title: Hybrid soup
pitfalls.body: A single agent that 'routes, plans, calls tools, and self-critiques' is impossible to debug. Compose patterns by chaining them, not by collapsing them into one prompt.
